heading: Naming Conventions
title: Poor name vs good name — and why it matters
rows: singular noun = the type (one specimen of the kind)
reader knows what it is; clean table name after mapping
STUDENT — ENROLLS — COURSE reads as a sentence
verb; a registrar can confirm or correct it on the spot
CUSTOMER — OWNS — ACCOUNT is plain English
stakeholders verify the model by reading it aloud
note: Singular-noun entities + verb relationships make the diagram self-explanatory and become clean table/column names after mapping.

heading: Design Issue: Attribute vs Entity
title: Attribute or its own entity? — the 'own data/relationships' test
rows: a plain value with no data of its own
has name, parent, icon; groups many products
nowhere to store category data if kept as text
has PAN, settlement account, many transactions
merchant details and links are lost
over-modelling — an entity adds needless complexity
can't relate its dishes or ratings
a customer has many; it has parts
can't store a customer's several addresses
usually just a tag on a restaurant
an extra table for no benefit
over-modelling if promoted to an entity
note: Model a concept as its own entity ONLY when it has its own attributes and/or relationships; otherwise an attribute is enough. Don't over-model.

heading: Degree Revisited: Binary, Ternary, n-ary
title: Real relationships classified by degree
rows: one fact links exactly two types
a two-way fact — most designs are binary
same entity type plays two roles
one fact ties three things together
a timetable fact of three at once
note: Degree = how many entity types the diamond touches. Binary (2) is by far the most common; ternary (3) is occasional; n > 3 is rare.

heading: Why a Ternary Is NOT Three Binaries
title: The combined fact three binaries silently lose
rows: that S supplied P specifically TO project J
which rider carried which order from which restaurant to which customer
which passenger rode which route with which rider on one trip
which doctor gave which drug to which patient
which teacher teaches which course in which room
which employee holds which role on which project
note: Pairwise facts can't capture that three entities were associated together in one instance. When the meaning is in the combination, use a ternary or an associative entity.

heading: Constraints & the Associative Entity
title: When a relationship should become an associative entity
rows: own attributes make a diamond awkward
the attribute 'grade' lives on the link
per-item data belongs on the link
clarifies the ternary and holds its data
keep as a plain binary relationship
note: Prefer binary. Promote a relationship to an associative (intermediate) entity when it needs its own attributes/relationships, or to make a higher-degree association clearer.

heading: Specialization & Generalization
title: Is-a hierarchies — and the direction of thinking
note: Specialization splits a superclass down; generalization combines similar entities up. Both produce an is-a hierarchy with attribute inheritance — inverse directions of one idea.

heading: Constraints: Disjoint/Overlap × Total/Partial
title: One example per constraint combination
rows: one type only; every account has one
exactly one; every employee is one of them
a vehicle is exactly one kind
a TA is both; a visitor is neither
can both buy & sell; a new user may be neither yet
a govt employee is also a citizen
a doctor can also be a patient; a visitor neither
one type, but some accounts fit none of these
note: Disjoint/overlap = how many subclasses an entity may join; total/partial = whether it must join one. The two are independent → four combinations.

heading: Attribute Inheritance & Specific Attributes
title: Inherit the shared, add the specific
note: Shared attributes (and relationships) live once in the superclass and are inherited by every subclass; each subclass adds only its own local attributes.

heading: The 7-Step Mapping Algorithm
title: Each ER construct → its relational result
rows: table with owner PK + partial key
DEPENDENT → DEPENDENT(emp_id FK, dep_name); PK=(emp_id, dep_name)
address → street, city; age is computed, never stored
note: The algorithm is mechanical: learn the seven cases (plus composite→flatten, derived→omit) and any ER diagram converts to tables the same way every time.

heading: Mapping 1:N — Foreign Key on the N Side
title: Where the foreign key lives in a 1:N relationship
note: The FK always goes on the N side, because each many-side row relates to exactly one partner — one FK column suffices. On the '1' side it would need a non-atomic multi-valued column (breaks 1NF).

heading: Mapping M:N — the Junction Table
title: Every M:N relationship becomes a junction table
note: One row per pair; the two PKs together form the composite primary key (each half a FK). Any attribute of the relationship (grade, quantity, date) lives in the junction table — never in either entity.

heading: Common Mapping Mistakes
title: The recurring mistakes — and their fixes
rows: M:N as a comma-list of ids in a column
can't aggregate one product; slow, buggy reports
one row must hold many ids
Storing a derived value (age, order total)
totals no longer match the line items
Multivalued attr kept as one field ('phones')
can't search or index one phone number
Weak entity without the owner's PK
Composite attr kept as one field ('address')
No primary key chosen for a table
note: All feel convenient at the keyboard and cost dearly later. Follow the algorithm: junction table for M:N, FK on the N side, omit derived data, separate table for multivalued/weak.
